concept.name: Large trader reporting
concept.definition: The CFTC's reporting system under which futures commission merchants, clearing members, foreign brokers, and traders must report positions at or above CFTC-set reporting levels — sizes of positions set by the exchanges and/or the CFTC at or above which traders or brokers must make daily reports of position size by commodity and delivery month and whether the position is controlled by a commercial or non-commercial trader.
concept.intuition: Once your position gets big enough to matter to the whole market, you can no longer stay anonymous — the regulator gets a daily look at exactly what you hold.
concept.mechanics: Clearing members and FCMs file daily large-trader reports for every account at or above the reporting level in a contract; traders themselves file identifying information (CFTC Form 40) on demand. The data feed market surveillance, position-limit enforcement, and the aggregated Commitments of Traders reports, and parallel regimes exist at the SEC (Rule 13h-1 Form 13H) for securities.
concept.failure_modes: Reporting levels are set per contract and can lag market growth, and accounts split across multiple FCMs or affiliates require aggregation to avoid undercounting; the system reports positions, not intent, so surveillance still must infer manipulation from the data.
concept.misconceptions: Large trader reports are confidential regulatory data, not public disclosures of individual positions — the public sees only aggregated Commitments of Traders figures; and the obligation binds the reporting firms as well as the traders, not just one side.
concept.example: A hedge fund holding 30,000 live-cattle futures across two FCMs exceeds the CFTC reporting level; both FCMs report the positions daily, and the fund files Form 40 identifying its controllers when asked.
